question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

EBULLIENT
option_2: Exuberant
option_4: Lethargic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Exuberant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ebullient (adjective) means overflowing with enthusiasm and high spirits; cheerful and full of energy. (उत्साही, उमंग से भरा)
◦ Example: The captain returned in an ebullient mood after the victory.

 

• Exuberant carries exactly this sense — full of lively energy and excitement. (उल्लासपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The exuberant crowd waited outside the stadium for hours.

 

• The word comes from Latin ebullire (to boil over), the same root as ebullition. The image of boiling over explains its use for feelings that cannot be contained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Gloomy (उदास, निराश): dark and depressed in mood — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Reserved (संकोची, अंतर्मुखी): slow to show feelings or opinions — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Lethargic (सुस्त, आलसी): sluggish and lacking energy.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of ebullient asked in SSC: effervescent, buoyant, elated, vivacious, animated.

 

• Antonyms: morose, despondent, sullen, apathetic, subdued.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

PERSPICACIOUS
option_2: Discerning
option_4: Careless
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Discerning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Perspicacious (adjective) means having keen insight and sound judgement; quick to notice and understand what is not obvious. (सूक्ष्मबुद्धि, तीक्ष्ण दृष्टि वाला)
◦ Example: A perspicacious reader would have noticed the contradiction on the first page.

 

• Discerning carries the same sense — showing good judgement and the ability to distinguish carefully. (विवेकशील)
◦ Example: The award is decided by a small panel of discerning critics.

 

• The word comes from Latin perspicere (to see through), the same root as perspective and perspicuity. Do not confuse perspicacious (sharp-witted) with perspicuous (clearly expressed).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Obtuse (मंदबुद्धि): slow to understand — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Gullible (भोला, जल्द बहकने वाला): easily deceived — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Careless (लापरवाह): not paying proper attention.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of perspicacious: astute, shrewd, sagacious, penetrating, judicious.

 

• Antonyms: dull, imperceptive, undiscerning, stupid, credulous.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

CURTAIL
option_2: Shorten
option_4: Abridge
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Extend.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Curtail (verb) means to cut short or reduce something, especially a right, a privilege or a period of time. (घटाना, संक्षिप्त करना)
◦ Example: Heavy rain forced the organisers to curtail the programme.

 

• Extend means to make something longer or larger in time or scope, and is therefore its direct opposite. (बढ़ाना, विस्तार करना)
◦ Example: The court extended the deadline by a fortnight.

 

• The word is related to Latin curtus (shortened), which also gives curt (rudely brief in speech).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Reduce (कम करना): to make smaller in size or amount — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Shorten (छोटा करना): to make shorter — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Abridge (संक्षिप्त करना): to shorten a text by condensing it — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Three options agree and one stands apart — the odd option is the answer. Other antonyms of curtail: prolong, lengthen, expand, augment, protract.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To burn the midnight oil
option_1: To waste resources on a hopeless cause
option_2: To work or study late into the night
option_4: To destroy records in order to hide the truth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To work or study late into the night.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To burn the midnight oil” means to work or study far into the night, usually because a task or an examination demands it. (रात देर तक पढ़ना या काम करना)
◦ Example: She burnt the midnight oil for a month before the interview.

 

• The expression belongs to the age of oil lamps, when working after dark literally meant consuming the household’s oil.

 

• Note that the idiom carries no suggestion of waste; the effort is purposeful, which is exactly what separates it from the first distractor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes futile expenditure — “to flog a dead horse” or “to pour money down the drain”.

 

• Option 3 describes lavish celebration — “to paint the town red”.

 

• Option 4 describes destroying evidence — “to cover one’s tracks”.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of hard work regularly tested: to put one’s shoulder to the wheel, to leave no stone unturned, to work one’s fingers to the bone, to sweat blood.

question: Choose the correct spelling of a word meaning ‘a mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh one’.
option_2: Euphimism
option_4: Uphemism
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Euphemism.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A euphemism is a mild, vague or roundabout expression substituted for one thought to be too harsh or blunt. (शिष्टोक्ति)
◦ Example: ‘Passed away’ is a common euphemism for ‘died’.

 

• The spelling follows the Greek elements eu- (good, pleasant) + pheme (speech) + -ism, giving eu-phem-ism — literally “good speech”. The middle syllable is therefore -phem-, with an ‘e’, and the ending is the ordinary -ism.

 

• The prefix eu- recurs in eulogy (praise), euphony (pleasant sound) and euthanasia (an easy death).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Euphimism — an ‘i’ wrongly replaces the ‘e’ of pheme.

 

• Option 3: Euphemisim — an extra ‘i’ has been inserted into the suffix.

 

• Option 4: Uphemism — the prefix eu- has lost its first letter.

 

NOTE

 

• Related figures of speech worth revising: dysphemism (a deliberately harsh substitute), circumlocution (a roundabout way of speaking), hyperbole (exaggeration), litotes (understatement through a negative).

question: Find the word that is spelled correctly and means ‘the quality of being deceitful or double-dealing’.
option_2: Duplicity
option_4: Duplisity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Duplicity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Duplicity means deceitfulness in speech or conduct, especially the practice of saying one thing while intending another. (कपट, दोहरा आचरण)
◦ Example: The negotiations broke down once his duplicity came to light.

 

• The spelling is fixed by the root duplex (twofold): dupl- + -icity, with a single ‘p’, an ‘i’ in the middle and a ‘c’ in the ending. Nouns of this pattern always end in -icity, never -isity — compare simplicity, publicity, authenticity.

 

• The literal idea of ‘doubleness’ survives in duplicate and duplex, and explains why the word means presenting two faces.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Dupplicity — the ‘p’ has been doubled without warrant.

 

• Option 3: Duplecity — an ‘e’ wrongly replaces the ‘i’.

 

• Option 4: Duplisity — an ‘s’ wrongly replaces the ‘c’ of the suffix.

 

NOTE

 

• Similar abstract nouns whose spellings are set in SSC: complicity (partnership in wrongdoing), mendacity (untruthfulness), rapacity (greed), tenacity (persistence), audacity (boldness).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

‘A person who attacks cherished beliefs and established institutions’.
option_2: Iconoclast
option_4: Purist
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Iconoclast.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An iconoclast is a person who attacks or seeks to overthrow traditional beliefs, customs and institutions. (परंपराओं पर प्रहार करने वाला)
◦ Example: He was an iconoclast who questioned every convention of the discipline.

 

• The word is built from Greek eikon (image) + klan (to break) — literally an image-breaker; the historical sense referred to those who destroyed religious images, and the modern sense extends this to attacking revered ideas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Conformist (रूढ़िवादी): one who follows accepted conventions without question — the opposite.

 

• Option 3: Loyalist (राजभक्त, निष्ठावान): one who remains faithful to an established government or ruler.

 

• Option 4: Purist (शुद्धतावादी): one who insists on strict correctness, especially in language or art.

 

NOTE

 

• The related cluster of ‘person who’ words: maverick (an independent-minded non-conformist), dissenter (one who disagrees with an official view), radical (one who favours thorough reform), reactionary (one who opposes change and prefers the past).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

‘Occurring, awarded or published after a person’s death’.
option_2: Postmortem
option_4: Postscript
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Posthumous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Posthumous (adjective) means happening, appearing or given after the death of the person concerned. (मरणोपरांत)
◦ Example: The soldier was awarded the medal posthumously.
◦ Example: Her last novel was a posthumous publication.

 

• The word comes from Latin postumus (last), later associated with humus (earth, hence burial) — which is why the modern spelling carries an h.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Postmortem (शवपरीक्षा): an examination of a body after death to determine its cause; also, a review of an event after it is over.

 

• Option 3: Posterity (भावी पीढ़ी): future generations, those who come after us.

 

• Option 4: Postscript (पुनश्च): a note added at the end of a letter after the signature, abbreviated P.S.

 

NOTE

 

• The prefix post- (after) is worth revising as a set: postpone (to put off), postdate, post-mortem, postgraduate, posterior — all opposed to ante-/pre- (before), as in antedate, antenatal, premonition.

question:
Choose the correct option:

 

His explanation was so implausible that the committee ____ it without further discussion.
option_2: dismissed
option_4: endorsed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. dismissed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The clue lies in the adjective implausible, which means not believable or convincing. An explanation that cannot be believed is rejected, and the phrase “without further discussion” confirms that it was set aside quickly.

 

• Dismiss (verb) here means to reject an idea as not worth considering. (खारिज करना)
◦ Complete sentence: His explanation was so implausible that the committee dismissed it without further discussion.

 

• The structure ‘so … that’ links a cause to its consequence, so the blank must follow logically from the negative quality named before it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Adopted (अपनाना): to accept and put into practice — the reverse of what an implausible explanation would receive.

 

• Option 3: Upheld (बरकरार रखना): to confirm or support a decision, especially in law.

 

• Option 4: Endorsed (समर्थन करना): to declare approval of something publicly.

 

NOTE

 

• In such fill-in-the-blank questions, first identify the valence of the sentence — whether the context is favourable or unfavourable. Here implausible is negative, so three positive options can be eliminated at a glance.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The chairman called for (1)/ an unanimous decision (2)/ on the question of (3)/ raising the annual subscription. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The choice between a and an depends on the sound with which the next word begins, not on its spelling. Although unanimous begins with the vowel letter u, it is pronounced “yoo-nan-i-mous”, beginning with the consonant sound /j/. It therefore takes a.
◦ Corrected: The chairman called for a unanimous decision on the question of raising the annual subscription.

 

• The same rule gives a university, a European country, a one-rupee coin, a useful book — and, conversely, an hour, an honest man, an M.A. degree, an X-ray, where a consonant letter carries a vowel sound.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: called for is the right phrasal verb for ‘demanded’.

 

• Part (3) is correct: on the question of is a well-formed prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct: the gerund raising rightly follows the preposition of.

 

NOTE

 

• Say the word aloud before choosing the article. If it begins with a vowel sound, use an; if with a consonant sound, use a. Spelling is a poor guide and is precisely what such questions exploit.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

The department will announce the examination results next week.
option_1: The examination results will announce by the department next week.
option_2: The examination results are going to announce next week by the department.
option_3: The examination results will be announced by the department next week.
option_4: The examination results would have been announced by the department next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The examination results will be announced by the department next week.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active verb will announce is in the simple future, whose passive is formed as:
◦ Object + will be + V3 + by + subject.

 

• Applying the rule:
◦ the object the examination results becomes the subject;
◦ will announce becomes will be announced;
◦ the department moves to the end with by, and the adverbial next week stays where it is.

 

• Note that will is never followed by been in the simple future passive; been belongs to the future perfect — will have been announced.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 omits be, leaving an active form with a passive meaning — as written, the results do the announcing.

 

• Option 2 substitutes are going to announce, which is both active in form and different in structure.

 

• Option 4 uses would have been announced, the passive of a perfect conditional, which contradicts the plain future of the original.

 

NOTE

 

• Future passives at a glance: simple future → will be + V3; future perfect → will have been + V3. The future continuous has no natural passive and is normally rewritten instead.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The scheme was neither (1)/ well designed or adequately funded, (2)/ and it collapsed quietly (3)/ within a single financial year. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Correlative conjunctions must be used in their fixed pairs. The word neither can be completed only by nor, never by or.
◦ Corrected: The scheme was neither well designed nor adequately funded, and it collapsed quietly within a single financial year.

 

• The elements joined must also be parallel in form; here well designed and adequately funded are both past participles, so the parallelism itself is sound — only the conjunction is at fault.

 

• Note that either pairs with or, and mixing the two pairs is the commonest error of this kind.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: neither is rightly placed after the verb was, so that both complements follow it.

 

• Part (3) is correct: collapsed quietly is a well-formed verb phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct: within a single financial year is an appropriate adverbial of time.

 

NOTE

 

• The fixed pairs to memorise: either … or, neither … nor, both … and, not only … but also, whether … or, no sooner … than, hardly/scarcely … when, such … that, so … that.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The villagers drew their water from the spring at the foot of the hill.
option_1: A clear spring rose among the rocks behind the temple.
option_2: The spring inside the old wall clock had snapped.
option_3: Cattle gathered at the spring throughout the dry months.
option_4: The spring that feeds the stream has never run dry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The spring inside the old wall clock had snapped.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, spring means a natural source of water rising from the ground. (जलस्रोत, झरना)

 

• In Option 2, spring means a coil of metal that returns to its shape after being compressed. (कमानी, स्प्रिंग) That is a wholly different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The remaining options all use spring in the sense of a water source, exactly as the highlighted word does.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: a clear spring rose among the rocks — a source of water; identical in meaning.

 

• Option 3: cattle gathered at the spring — again a water source.

 

• Option 4: the spring that feeds the stream — the same sense once more.

 

NOTE

 

• The word has two further senses — the season after winter and the verb meaning to leap — which makes it a favourite in such questions. Always fix the sense of the highlighted word first, then look for the option that departs from it.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The main gate is kept locked after ten by the night watchman.
option_1: The night watchman keeps the main gate locked after ten.
option_2: The night watchman is keeping the main gate locked after ten.
option_3: The night watchman kept the main gate locked after ten.
option_4: The main gate is locked by the night watchman who keeps it after ten.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The night watchman keeps the main gate locked after ten.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — the night watchman — becomes the subject, and the passive subject the main gate becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb is kept is in the simple present, so the active verb is keeps, agreeing with the singular subject.
◦ Active: The night watchman keeps the main gate locked after ten.

 

• The word locked is not part of the passive verb; it is an object complement describing the state of the gate, and it therefore remains unchanged in the active sentence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 turns a habitual action into one in progress at the moment of speaking.

 

• Option 3 shifts the sentence into the past, altering the time of the action.

 

• Option 4 keeps the first clause passive and merely adds a relative clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs such as keep, make, find, consider, call, elect, paint take an object + complement: They elected him captain → He was elected captain. The complement never changes place when the voice is changed.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The residents strongly objected to be moved to a temporary shelter.
option_2: against being moved
option_4: to be moving
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. to being moved.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the phrase ‘object to’, the word to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. A preposition must be followed by a noun or a gerund (-ing form), and since the residents are the ones being moved, the passive gerund being moved is required.
◦ Corrected: The residents strongly objected to being moved to a temporary shelter.

 

• Test it by substituting a plain noun: They objected to the transfer. The sentence works, which proves that to** here is a preposition.

 

• The same pattern governs look forward to, be accustomed to, be averse to, with a view to, be opposed to, confess to — all followed by -ing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘against being moved’ uses the wrong preposition; one objects to, not against.

 

• Option 3: ‘for being moved’ likewise takes a preposition that object does not govern.

 

• Option 4: ‘to be moving’ keeps the infinitive and is active in sense, which reverses the meaning — the residents were not doing the moving.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the two uses of to: as an infinitive marker it is followed by V1 (he agreed to go); as a preposition it is followed by a gerund (*he is used to going***). Only the second is tested here.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India’s handloom tradition is less a single craft than a federation of regional grammars — the ikat of Odisha, the jamdani of Bengal, the pashmina of Kashmir — each with its own vocabulary of motif, count and weave. To describe such work as textile production alone is to miss its character, for a handloom fabric records a system of knowledge in which dyeing, warping, motif and drape are learnt together, usually within a family, over years for which no formal certificate exists. That embeddedness is also the sector’s vulnerability. Powerloom imitations reproduce the surface pattern at a fraction of the cost and reach the market first; the weaver, paid by the piece and rarely owning the yarn he works with, absorbs the loss. Geographical Indication tags have been secured for many of these weaves, yet a tag protects a name rather than a livelihood, and its enforcement rests with those least able to go to court. Revival efforts carry hazards of their own. Design intervention from outside can restore demand, but where the designer dictates and the weaver merely executes, the craft is preserved as a technique while its authorship quietly changes hands. Nor is nostalgia a strategy: an insistence that weavers reproduce only ‘authentic’ historical motifs freezes a living practice into heritage, denying it the innovation by which every tradition has always renewed itself. What has worked, where it has worked, is neither charity nor curation but a change in the weaver’s position within the chain — cooperatives that hold yarn stocks, direct access to buyers, credit that does not depend on the trader, and pricing that treats skill as skilled labour rather than as rustic charm. The choice, then, is not between preserving the handloom and modernising it. It is between a modernity in which the weaver remains a supplier of cheap dexterity and one in which he is the author of what he makes.

 

What tension does the passage highlight regarding revival efforts in the handloom sector?
option_1: Design help from outside can restore demand while quietly transferring authorship away from the weaver
option_2: Weavers refuse to accept any change in traditional motifs
option_3: Cooperatives are unable to obtain yarn at reasonable prices
option_4: Buyers prefer powerloom fabric for its superior quality
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Design help from outside can restore demand while quietly transferring authorship away from the weaver.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage concedes the benefit first — design intervention from outside can restore demand — and then names the cost: where the designer dictates and the weaver merely executes, the craft survives as a technique while its authorship quietly changes hands.

 

• That double movement, a gain accompanied by a loss, is precisely what makes it a tension rather than a simple objection.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 reverses the passage, which criticises the demand that weavers reproduce only authentic motifs.

 

• Option 3 concerns yarn stocks, which the passage mentions as part of the remedy, not the problem with revival.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the text: powerloom goods are described as cheap imitations that merely reach the market first.

 

NOTE

 

• A question asking for a tension always has a two-sided answer. Options that state only a benefit or only a harm are, for that reason alone, unlikely to be correct.

It is between a modernity in which the weaver remains a supplier of cheap dexterity and one in which he is the author of what he makes.

 

Which of the following best reflects the passage’s view of Geographical Indication tags?
option_1: They have effectively ended powerloom imitation
option_2: They are opposed by most weavers as an unnecessary burden
option_3: They protect a name without securing the weaver’s livelihood
option_4: They remove the need for cooperatives altogether
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They protect a name without securing the weaver’s livelihood.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage acknowledges that such tags have been secured for many weaves, and then states the limitation in the same sentence: a tag protects a name rather than a livelihood.

 

• A second limitation follows immediately — enforcement rests with those least able to go to court — which explains why the protection remains largely nominal for the weaver.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is contradicted by the passage, in which powerloom imitations continue to reach the market first.

 

• Option 2 attributes to weavers an opposition that the passage never reports.

 

• Option 4 confuses the tag with the structural remedies listed later, of which cooperatives are one.

 

NOTE

 

• Where a passage uses “yet” or “however” immediately after conceding something, the clause that follows almost always contains the answer.

option_2: It freezes a living practice into heritage and denies it the power to innovate
option_3: It confuses buyers about the true origin of a fabric
option_4: It lengthens the years of training a weaver must undergo
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It freezes a living practice into heritage and denies it the power to innovate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage says plainly that nostalgia is not a strategy: such an insistence freezes a living practice into heritage, denying it the innovation by which every tradition has always renewed itself.

 

• The objection is therefore not to tradition but to fixing it. A craft treated as a museum piece loses the very capacity that kept it alive.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces the cost of dyes, which the passage nowhere discusses.

 

• Option 3 concerns the confusion of buyers — an issue the passage raises in connection with imitations, not with authentic motifs.

 

• Option 4 refers to the years of training, mentioned only to show how the knowledge is transmitted.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage rejects two opposite errors — here uncritical modernisation on one side and frozen nostalgia on the other — expect a question on each. Locate the sentence in which the second error is named.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India’s handloom tradition is less a single craft than a federation of regional grammars — the ikat of Odisha, the jamdani of Bengal, the pashmina of Kashmir — each with its own vocabulary of motif, count and weave. To describe such work as textile production alone is to miss its character, for a handloom fabric records a system of knowledge in which dyeing, warping, motif and drape are learnt together, usually within a family, over years for which no formal certificate exists. That embeddedness is also the sector’s vulnerability. Powerloom imitations reproduce the surface pattern at a fraction of the cost and reach the market first; the weaver, paid by the piece and rarely owning the yarn he works with, absorbs the loss. Geographical Indication tags have been secured for many of these weaves, yet a tag protects a name rather than a livelihood, and its enforcement rests with those least able to go to court. Revival efforts carry hazards of their own. Design intervention from outside can restore demand, but where the designer dictates and the weaver merely executes, the craft is preserved as a technique while its authorship quietly changes hands. Nor is nostalgia a strategy: an insistence that weavers reproduce only ‘authentic’ historical motifs freezes a living practice into heritage, denying it the innovation by which every tradition has always renewed itself. What has worked, where it has worked, is neither charity nor curation but a change in the weaver’s position within the chain — cooperatives that hold yarn stocks, direct access to buyers, credit that does not depend on the trader, and pricing that treats skill as skilled labour rather than as rustic charm. The choice, then, is not between preserving the handloom and modernising it. It is between a modernity in which the weaver remains a supplier of cheap dexterity and one in which he is the author of what he makes.

 

According to the passage, what has actually improved the weaver’s condition where improvement has occurred?
option_2: Stricter penalties imposed on individual buyers
option_3: Complete state ownership of looms and yarn
option_4: A change in the weaver’s position within the chain — cooperatives, direct buyers, credit and fair pricing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A change in the weaver’s position within the chain — cooperatives, direct buyers, credit and fair pricing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that what has worked is neither charity nor curation but a change in the weaver’s position within the chain, and then lists the measures: cooperatives that hold yarn stocks, direct access to buyers, credit independent of the trader, and pricing that treats skill as skilled labour.

 

• The common thread is bargaining power. Each measure removes one dependence — on the trader for yarn, for credit, or for access to the market.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 names precisely what the passage rules out with the words neither charity nor curation.

 

• Option 2 proposes penalties on buyers, a measure the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 3 goes far beyond the text; state ownership is nowhere recommended.

 

NOTE

 

• Sentences built on “neither … nor … but” are almost always the thesis of a paragraph. The words after but carry the author’s own position and, very often, the answer.

What stance does the author finally take on the modernisation of handloom weaving?
option_1: Modernisation should be resisted so that the craft may survive unchanged
option_2: The real question is not whether to modernise but what place the weaver holds in the modern chain
option_3: Only export markets can rescue the sector from decline
option_4: Handloom weaving should be maintained purely as a heritage practice
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The real question is not whether to modernise but what place the weaver holds in the modern chain.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The closing lines settle the matter: the choice is not between preserving the handloom and modernising it, but between a modernity in which the weaver remains a supplier of cheap dexterity and one in which he is the author of what he makes.

 

• The author therefore treats modernisation as inevitable and shifts the argument to its terms — who decides, who profits and who is credited.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the position of nostalgia, which the passage has already dismissed.

 

• Option 3 introduces export markets, which the passage does not discuss.

NOTE

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to the attendant, “Please shut the window.”
option_1: He said the attendant that please shut the window.
option_2: He requested the attendant to shut the window.
option_3: He told the attendant that he shut the window.
option_4: He requested the attendant that he should please shut the window.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He requested the attendant to shut the window.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence is an imperative softened by please, which makes it a request. Such sentences are reported with a suitable reporting verb — request, ask, order, advise, forbid — followed by an object + to-infinitive.
◦ Indirect: He requested the attendant to shut the window.

 

• Three changes follow automatically:
◦ the connective that is not used with an imperative;
◦ the word please is absorbed into the verb requested and is dropped;
◦ the inverted commas disappear.

 

• For a negative command, the pattern is ‘not to + V1’: He requested the attendant not to shut the window.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses said with a direct object and retains please, both of which are wrong.

 

• Option 3 turns the request into a statement of fact.

 

• Option 4 mixes the that-clause with a request and keeps please.

 

NOTE

 

• Choose the reporting verb to match the force of the original: ordered (a command), requested (a polite appeal), advised (a suggestion), forbade (a prohibition), implored/begged (an earnest plea).

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

She said, “I had already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.”
option_1: She said that she has already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.
option_2: She said that she had already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.
option_3: She said that she already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.
option_4: She said that she had already been dispatching the reply before the reminder arrived.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She said that she had already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported words are already in the past perfect (had dispatched), and the past perfect has no earlier tense to move back to. It therefore remains unchanged in indirect speech.

 

• Only two changes are needed: the pronoun I becomes she, and the connective that is supplied in place of the inverted commas.
◦ Indirect: She said that she had already dispatched the reply before the reminder arrived.

 

• This is the one tense that candidates most often “correct” unnecessarily; back-shift applies only where a further step back is possible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 moves the verb forward to the present perfect, which no rule permits after a past reporting verb.

 

• Option 3 reduces it to the simple past and loses the sequence of the two past actions.

 

• Option 4 changes a completed action into one in progress.

 

NOTE

 

• Forms that stay unchanged in reported speech: past perfect, past perfect continuous, and the modals would, could, might, should, ought to, must (in the sense of obligation).

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He declared that never before had the club won three finals in a row.
option_1: “Never before has the club won three finals in a row,” he declared.
option_2: “Never before the club has won three finals in a row,” he declared.
option_3: “Never before had the club won three finals in a row,” he declared.
option_4: “The club has never before won three finals in a row?” he declared.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. “Never before has the club won three finals in a row,” he declared.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The past reporting verb declared had back-shifted the original present perfect into the past perfect. Converting to direct speech undoes that step: had won returns to has won.

 

• The inversion demanded by the opening adverbial “Never before” must be preserved, so the auxiliary still stands before the subject — has the club won.
◦ Direct: “Never before has the club won three finals in a row,” he declared.

 

• Inverted commas, the capital letter and the comma before the reporting clause complete the conversion; the sentence remains a statement, so no question mark is used.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 abandons the inversion and places the subject before the auxiliary.

 

• Option 3 keeps the back-shifted past perfect, so no conversion has taken place.

 

• Option 4 turns a declaration into a question, contradicting the reporting verb declared.

 

NOTE

 

• Inversion belongs to the structure of the sentence, not to the reporting, and is therefore carried across unchanged in both directions: He said that only then did he realise the mistake → “Only then did I realise the mistake,” he said.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The clock on the tower in the market square had not struck the hour for over thirty years.

 

A. A retired signalman, who had once maintained railway clocks, offered to examine the mechanism.

 

B. He found that nothing stood between silence and sound except a broken pin and a seized bearing.

 

C. The traders had grown so used to the quiet that few could recall what the bell had sounded like.

 

D. Two afternoons of work and a borrowed can of oil were enough to set the hands moving again.

 

S2. The hour is now heard across three streets, and the square keeps time by it once more.
option_2: C-A-B-D
option_4: A-B-C-D
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. C-A-B-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – C – A – B – D – S2, and the paragraph moves from situation → its effect → the offer → the diagnosis → the repair.

 

• S1 states the situation — a clock silent for thirty years.
◦ C describes the effect of that silence on the traders, and follows S1 naturally.
◦ A introduces the signalman, who must be named before he can be referred to again.
◦ B begins with “He found”, and the pronoun He can only stand for the signalman of A.
◦ D gives the repair that the diagnosis in B made possible, and leads into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-C-B-D) separates A from B, leaving the pronoun He stranded across an unrelated sentence.

 

• Option 3 (C-B-A-D) uses the pronoun He before the person has been introduced.

 

• Option 4 (A-B-C-D) places the traders’ long habit of silence after the clock has already been examined.

 

NOTE

 

• The noun-before-pronoun rule settles most rearrangement questions: a sentence beginning with He, She, It, They or This must follow the sentence that names what the pronoun stands for.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Nutmeg was once worth more by weight than gold in the markets of Europe.

 

A. The trees grew, so far as anyone then knew, on a handful of small islands in the eastern seas.

 

B. Whoever held those islands could therefore set very nearly whatever price the trade would bear.

 

C. Seedlings smuggled out in the eighteenth century were planted elsewhere, and the monopoly collapsed within a generation.

 

D. Wars were fought and treaties signed over specks of land a few kilometres across.

 

S2. The spice now costs less than the paper on which its history is written.
option_2: A-B-D-C
option_4: D-A-B-C
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-B-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – B – D – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from the fact → its cause → the consequence → the extreme consequence → the collapse.

 

• S1 states the fact — an extraordinary price.
◦ A supplies the cause: the trees grew in only a few places.
◦ B begins with “Whoever held those islands” and contains “therefore”, both of which tie it directly to A.
◦ D carries that consequence to its extreme — wars and treaties over tiny islands.
◦ C ends the story: once seedlings were smuggled out, the monopoly, and with it the price, collapsed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) opens with “those islands” before any islands have been mentioned.

 

• Option 3 (A-D-B-C) places the wars before the explanation of why the islands were worth fighting over.

 

• Option 4 (D-A-B-C) begins with the wars, leaving the reader to guess what was at stake.

 

NOTE

 

• Two signposts decide this question: the demonstrative “those islands” must follow the sentence that introduces them, and “therefore” must follow the fact from which the inference is drawn.
